name: Palestine
headline: No law we found gives Palestinian patients a copy of their record; the ministry's system runs in 15 hospitals and, it says, Gaza's was lost.

access.summary: We found no Palestinian law that gives patients a right to see or copy their file: the 2004 Public Health Law lists five patient rights, none of them access. The government Hukumati portal shows test results, insurance status and referrals only.
detail: Article 60 of Public Health Law No. 20 of 2004 gives patients in a health facility rights to emergency care, an explanation of treatment, consent to research, privacy and dignity, and to complain. It does not mention seeing or copying the medical file.

Decree-Law No. 31 of 2018 obliges every provider to keep a medical file recording all procedures and care (Article 4). It sets no right for the patient to read or receive a copy, and no fee or deadline.

In June 2025 the health minister said citizens can check test results, such as COVID tests, health insurance status and medical referrals on the Hukumati portal, and that lab and radiology results would be added soon. Whether they went live is not verified.
The ministry runs 19 hospitals and 450 primary care clinics, by the minister's figures for 2024. With no enforceable right, the score stays in the 15 to 35 band.

control.summary: Patients have no opt-out, no consent setting and no access log in the ministry's systems; none was found. The 2018 decree-law bars staff from revealing patient secrets, except to competent bodies in cases set by law.
detail: Article 10(5) of Decree-Law No. 31 of 2018 forbids anyone in a medical profession from disclosing a patient's secrets, except to competent authorities and in cases the law sets. Article 60 of the Public Health Law gives a right to privacy and dignity.
Consent rules in the 2018 decree-law cover examination and treatment (written consent for surgery), not who may see or share the record.

The ministry's Avicenna system is linked to the health insurance system, the electronic referral application, the medical imaging archive and lab devices. Whether one patient file opens across hospitals by national ID is not verified.
No patient-visible access log, opt-out or consent tool was found in ministry statements or in the law texts read.

privacy.summary: Palestine has no comprehensive data protection law or regulator; a 2025 draft naming health data as sensitive went to public consultation. Protection rests on a medical secrecy duty, a cybercrime privacy offence and a 2019 Cabinet decision, and no breach notification duty was found.
detail: A Palestinian law firm wrote in July 2026 that Palestine has no standalone, comprehensive personal data protection law. Rules are spread across the Basic Law, a 2019 Cabinet decision, the cybercrime law, the electronic transactions law and the 2025 e-commerce law.
The draft data protection decree-law was open for comment from 30 October to 8 November 2025. It defines health data, including data on health care received, as sensitive.
Article 22 of Decree-Law No. 10 of 2018 on cybercrime bans arbitrary or unlawful interference in a person's privacy and punishes publishing material about private life with prison or fines.

In 2022 a ransomware attack encrypted health ministry information systems and databases. A government committee said all data was recovered, with systems restored to their state of 25 August 2022, the day before the attack. No breach notification duty for health data was found.

commercial.summary: A 2019 Cabinet decision bans companies and institutions from using service users' personal data for commercial purposes without prior permission. It names no specific penalty, and no rule on health data brokers, health apps or de-identified data sales was found.
detail: Cabinet Decision No. 3 of 2019 has two articles. The first forbids using citizens' direct or indirect personal data, held by service providers, for commercial purposes without their prior permission, under legal liability.
A July 2026 law firm analysis says the decision carries no direct penalty and has stayed largely absent from practice.
No health-specific rule on selling patient data, marketing use, data brokers or consumer health apps was found.

journey.summary: The ministry's Avicenna system runs in 15 hospitals, 4 health directorates and 7 clinics, and a DHIS2 patient file runs in 7 directorates. The ministry says the war caused electronic systems to collapse in a number of Gaza facilities.
detail: In June 2025 the minister said Avicenna was moved to a new environment and relinked to health insurance, electronic referrals, the imaging archive and lab devices. A web version and a disaster recovery centre were in progress.

In November 2025 the ministry said a computerised patient file on DHIS2 runs in seven health directorates, and an electronic referral system is being built. A 2022 trial paper says the maternal and child eRegistry, built with the ministry for public primary care, is the routine health information system in Palestine.

Before the war, a 2023 ministry plan for the southern governorates (Gaza) listed different systems, E-Hos for hospitals and Clinic Care for primary care, run unevenly. Their current status was not found.
No link between ministry systems and NGO, UNRWA or private providers, or East Jerusalem hospitals, was found.

clinical.summary: Clinicians in the 15 ministry hospitals on Avicenna can use one system with linked imaging and lab results. WHO reports 18 of Gaza's 36 hospitals partly functioning at end 2025, and no exchange with other providers was found.
detail: Avicenna connects hospital records with the imaging archive and lab devices, according to the minister. Whether clinicians in one hospital can open a file created in another is not verified.

WHO reported that all 36 Gaza hospitals were damaged and 18 were partly functioning at 31 December 2025. A 2026 World Bank, EU and UN assessment lists restoring health information systems among Gaza's recovery needs.

WHO says movement restrictions delay West Bank patients' access to specialised care in east Jerusalem. No source was found on whether east Jerusalem hospitals connect to ministry record systems; not verified.

research.summary: Health research needs approval from ministry ethics committees under 2025 instructions, with patient privacy studies and file reviews sent to the higher committee. Drug trials need written informed consent, but no general opt-out from secondary use of records exists.
detail: Instructions No. 10 of 2025 set a ministry technical committee and a higher technical committee. Research touching patient privacy or rights, or needing a review of ministry files, goes to the higher committee, which approves, rejects or asks for changes. Approval lasts one year.
Article 60(3) of the Public Health Law gives patients the right to agree to or refuse taking part in research or training in a health facility.
Decree-Law No. 21 of 2016 bars drug studies on people without voluntary, written, informed consent, and bars using samples beyond the study's stated purposes.
Score: base 40, plus 3 each for an ethics body, statutory secrecy and a consent route. No public register of data uses was found.

ai.summary: No rule on AI used in clinical care, and no device regulation of AI software, was found. A national team approved a general AI strategy and policy for Cabinet adoption; Cabinet adoption is not verified.
detail: The telecommunications ministry reported that the national AI team approved the final AI strategy and recommended Cabinet adoption, together with an AI policy and an open data policy. The page is undated and is not specific to health.
No health ministry instruction on AI in diagnosis, change control for AI software or human oversight was found.

With no AI device rules in force and Cabinet adoption of the strategy not verified, the score sits in the 15 to 30 band for non-EU countries with nothing in force, level with Lebanon's 20 (plans only) and below Libya's 25 (adopted charter naming health).
